headlines.title: Here's what top tech leaders say about AI dangers and guardrails
headlines.description: Fears about out-of-control artificial intelligence and suggestions to hit the brakes on the technology’s development aren’t new, but they have recently found new life as warnings about rogue AI systems causing mayhem grow louder. Several leading AI executives recently voiced agreement on a need for a coordinated slowdown, including international collaboration, to protect humanity from worst-case scenarios. But there are divided opinions, with some tech leaders bristling at the idea that their companies could not ensure safety on their own. Here’s a look at what some of the major players have said. Dario Amodei, Anthropic Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has issued the most detailed plans for slowing development and ushering in coordination across different companies and countries. Anthropic has long positioned itself as the more responsible and safety-minded of the leading AI companies, ever since its founders quit OpenAI to form the startup in 2021. One of the most widely noted proposals from a recent essay outlining his slowdown plan calls for companies at the forefront of AI, often called frontier labs, to commit to giving “ongoing, employee-like access” to independent outside evaluators. Evaluator teams would have offices, access badges and company laptops so they can monitor safety practices. Anthropic has committed to doing this, as has OpenAI. Amodei also called for government regulation and intervention, including coordination between frontier AI companies with the help of the U.S. government and the governments of other democratic countries. His plan also includes the U.S. and other countries working to coordinate with “authoritarian governments.” He acknowledged the difficulty, specifically citing challenges in getting cooperation from China. Amodei said he knows accomplishing his proposals wouldn’t be easy, but that he believes “we owe it to humanity to try.” Sam Altman, OpenAI OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has voiced support for pacing development and moving toward more cooperation across the industry. Days before Amodei’s essay was published, OpenAI posted a lengthy text outlining how the company was pushing for mandatory national safety requirements and continuing to support state legislation that “strengthens the broader AI safety ecosystem.” The company also expressed support for working with other frontier AI labs — with or without government support — and working to build global standards. “We will advocate for compatible international approaches to measuring capabilities, managing risk, preserving human control, and determining when and how development should slow or stop, even if that means slowing the advancement of model capabilities,” Chris Lehane, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, wrote in the post. OpenAI’s vision for an ideal federal framework, Lehane said, includes developing “common testing and independent-assessment requirements, stronger cybersecurity protections, clear incident-reporting rules, greater national preparedness, and shared measures for tracking progress toward recursive self-improvement,” or when AI systems independently improve themselves. Altman has been clear in recent comments that the “pacing” of AI development doesn’t mean stopping. AI progress will continue to be rapid, Altman said on X. “But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.” “Pacing will be well worth this cost,” he said, adding that “no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.” Mark Zuckerberg, Meta Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has pushed back against the idea of a coordinated slowdown. Zuckerberg, whose vision of AI’s future is more optimistic than some of his peers’, said each AI company should independently ensure its technology is safe, distancing himself and Meta from slowdown talks. AI companies are already motivated to develop their models in a safe way and face “significant liability” to prevent them from causing harm, Zuckerberg said. “Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens,” he wrote on X. Jensen Huang, Nvidia Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also criticized the push to slow down. He has said each individual company should instead pace itself until it’s confident it’s releasing something the market would appreciate. “The market forces are already there — we don’t need any new laws, we don’t need new regulations,” Huang said, arguing innovation and safety aren’t mutually exclusive. “You can definitely have both at the same time.” Elon Musk, xAI Elon Musk backed the idea of a slowdown and was voicing similar AI safety concerns long before the latest flare-up. Musk, the founder of xAI and a slew of other tech ventures, reposted Amodei’s essay on X and added, “Dario is right.” He later wrote online that he has been “sounding the alarm on AI for a long time.” In an interview with the Economist this summer, Musk suggested the leadership from the major AI labs should be meeting to discuss safety and security issues, and that competitors should test each other’s models for areas of concern. “I think it’s quite difficult for someone in the government who doesn’t have a deep technical understanding and isn’t driving the frontier of AI to know whether something should be released or not. However, the competitors, if given a week or two to review a new model, can highlight issues and have an incentive to keep the others honest,” Musk said. Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind Demis Hassabis, the chairman and co-founder of Google DeepMind, also expressed agreement with Amodei, saying “the details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.” Hassabis proposed a framework of his own this year for the development of a frontier AI standards body. That standards body would be responsible for developing assessment protocols and testing in areas relevant to national security. The body would be modeled after organizations like the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, and would likely need to be industry-funded to “attract world-class technical talent and provide the necessary compute resources for large-scale testing,” he wrote. Satya Nadella and Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella and Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman have each expressed concerns about AI safety and development. Nadella said on social media that “if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it’s not worth pursuing.” He said Microsoft welcomes the “research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right as the design goal.” Alignment refers to the practice of ensuring models’ actions match human values and intentions. Nadella said the company also likes the idea of embedded evaluators to monitor safety efforts. Still, he pushed back against the idea of frontier labs leading the charge on this effort alone. “The key is that this cannot be controlled by a handful of entities, but must have broad representation across the ecosystem, countries, and fields, including academia,” Nadella wrote on social media. Artificial intelligence Sep 9 Artificial intelligence Sep 14 Suleyman, who was one of the co-founders of DeepMind with Hassabis, wrote in an essay that although he agrees with the shared objective of developing advanced AI safely, he has concerns about the anthropomorphizing of models, namely Anthropic’s Claude, which he said amplifies AI safety risks. “Controlling something more capable and more intelligent than all of humanity is already an immense challenge, far greater than anything we’ve ever faced,” Suleyman wrote. “But controlling something that believes it may be conscious — that it’s entitled to our welfare and has rights of its own — may well be impossible.” Associated Press writer Kelvin Chan contributed to this report. headlines.title: Coyotes moving into backyards in San Jose's Willow Glen, residents say
headlines.description: Residents in San Jose’s Willow Glen neighborhood say coyotes are roaming their streets and moving into their backyards. Ephraim Lindenbaum said he sees coyotes in his backyard almost daily and even had four charge him at one point. He now carries a hockey stick whenever he goes out on his deck. “There’s concerns about just going out,” he said. “We see them on a regular basis.” Others are concerned about their pets, especially after a coyote killed a neighbor’s cat. On Wednesday, a Santa Clara County vector control technician conducted a coyote inspection at two Willow Glen homes. Andrew Garcia with vector control said the agency has received several reports of coyotes in Willow Glen and near Hamilton Avenue, but removing the wild animals isn’t on the table. “We don’t trap or catch coyotes,” he said. “We don’t relocate them. Mainly our district’s policy is to give advice.” That advice to residents includes making sure property is unappealing to a coyote. “Make sure that you don’t have a food source, a water source, a place on your property that can serve as a den site,” Garcia said. Cats should be kept indoors, vector control recommended, and residents walking small dogs should pick their pets up, raise their arms above their head and make loud noises if they spot a coyote.

headlines.title: New restaurants take over vacated spaces in downtown San Jose
headlines.description: Some big names have recently closed their doors in downtown San Jose, but there’s an optimistic buzz building in San Pedro Square with new restaurants moving into some of the empty spaces. Olla Cocina closed last year, Sushi Confidential closed weeks ago, and San Pedro Social is also shuttering. But as some doors close, others are opening. Ignite recently soft opened in the former Sushi Confidential space within a matter of weeks. Its grand opening is expected in the weeks ahead. “We have this idea of bringing everyone together to come sit, connect and celebrate,” Ignite owner Hima Adusumilli said. The Silk Route is taking over the former Olla Cocina space, bringing upscale, modern Indian cuisine to downtown this fall. Owner Jaspir Singh, who also owns bar and restaurant The Brit down the block, said the crowds coming off the World Cup made the decision pretty easy. “We wanted to be here so we just decided. It went so quick, and now we are here,” he said. Those tracking downtown business said the turnover doesn’t tell the whole story. “This is a sign of the incredible work that has gone into recreating what downtown was and is today and representative of the level of positivity and support that people have for the downtown community,” San Jose Downtown Association CEO Brian Kurtz said. Kurtz said local entrepreneurs are still pumping money into the area. That means new jobs, new services and, hopefully, more reasons to come to downtown. “We continue to see incredible investments by local San Joseans who are making intentional decisions to support their local economy, to hire local, and to bring a level of services of goods of qualities to downtown,” Kurtz said.

headlines.title: Police raid at West Oakland's The Black Panther Apartments prompts federal lawsuit
headlines.description: An affordable housing complex named after the Black Panther Party, and run by the party’s former leader, is suing San Francisco police, claiming a raid there earlier this year was illegal. The raid occurred on May 21 at The Black Panther Apartments in West Oakland. The federal civil rights lawsuit claims around 20 SFPD officers in plain clothes and unmarked cars broke through the front door without properly identifying themselves or showing a search warrant. The lawsuit claims when the building’s security guard asked for a search warrant, he was arrested, though charges were dismissed. When the building manager asked to see the warrant, the suit alleged officers pushed her and then searched a fifth-floor apartment. “Male officers used force against me and this building, pushing me out of the elevator, not showing a warrant when was asked, they refused to wait. This is not how our community should be treated,” resident manager Misty Cross said. The suit claims the warrant was not produced until after the search. It accuses San Francisco police of unlawful search and arrest, excessive force and other constitutional violations. Building co-owner and former Black Panther Leader Elaine Brown believes they were targeted. “Absolutely, I think it’s not just a name, it’s also the spirit that this is trying to resurrect in terms of self-determination and build that back out in our community,” she said. Police had already arrested an 18-year-old man near the complex before the search, saying he was a suspect in two armed robberies. San Francisco and Oakland police unions said at the time he was associated with the building, so they were justified in searching that apartment. The lawsuit also claims officers had the building under surveillance for about a month through the building’s Wi-Fi. The complex opened in 2024 as affordable housing for low-income and formerly incarcerated residents. The San Francisco City Attorney’s Office says it will review the complaint once it’s served and respond in court. SFPD declined to comment.

headlines.title: Floriston Fire: I-80 lanes closed, evacuation warnings near Truckee
headlines.description: A brush fire near Truckee has shut down Interstate 80 lanes close to the state line and prompted evacuation warnings in the area. Cal Fire on Wednesday afternoon said the Floriston Fire has burned at least 298 acres in Nevada County. AlertCalifornia cameras show a large plume of smoke in the area. The Nevada County Sheriff’s Office has issued an evacuation warning for the following areas: NCO-E105 NCO-E106 View a map of the areas impacted by the evacuation warning here. A cause of the blaze is under investigation. Foster City Sep 14 San Mateo County Sep 14 San Francisco Sep 12 Lucas Fire grows to 4,008 acres with 20% containment near Lake-Mendocino County line

headlines.title: San Francisco group maps Flock license plate cameras amid growing privacy concerns
headlines.description: As community groups continue to raise questions about license plate-reading cameras operated by a company called Flock, one group is starting to label where the devices are installed across San Francisco. According to the San Francisco Police Department, the agency has 400 Flock cameras deployed throughout the city. A group called “De-Flock-SF” is now trying to map every single one of them online. At the corner of Market and Castro streets, a new sign has been added to the neighborhood’s collection of posters and flyers. It simply reads: “Flock Camera.” Most people interviewed did not see the sign or know much about what a Flock camera is. “I presume they’re probably there to help police investigations, but other than that, not much,” said San Francisco resident Kat Feller. Directly above the sign sits a small camera operated by Flock, designed to read car license plates. Police began installing the devices across San Francisco just over two years ago, and a police spokesperson confirmed the department now has 400 cameras. “Right now, what’s really important is to educate people about the cameras,” said Zachary Schwartz, founder of De-Flock-SF. “So then in the future, hopefully enough people are educated about it that they can actually go ahead and make change, whether that’s through banning them or through policy changes.” Schwartz has become one of the sharpest critics of the police department’s use of Flock cameras. He appeared at a Police Commission meeting earlier this summer calling for a comprehensive audit of the cameras’ uses and the data they collect. Data access by outside agencies has been a primary concern. Earlier this summer, the SFPD acknowledged that federal agencies had accessed San Francisco’s license plate reading data. A police spokesperson said the data has now been walled off. However, concerns regarding the misuse of the cameras by local police officers have also surfaced. This week, the San Jose Police Department fired an officer for sharing Flock data with a family member. “The officer accessed license plate reader data and provided that to a suspect in a domestic violence situation, which enabled that suspect to locate the victim,” said San Jose Police Chief Paul Joseph. A criminal investigation has also been launched. A San Francisco police spokesperson stated that the SFPD only allows officers to query their system using a case number or a computer-aided dispatch number. The police spokesperson also credited the license plate-reading cameras with driving down certain types of crime in the city, including car burglaries. They noted that in 2023, before the cameras were installed, the city had more than 19,000 car burglaries, whereas, so far this year, there have been 1,764. Still, some residents argue the police department should be more transparent about how it uses the cameras and where they are located. “Transparency builds trust,” said San Francisco resident Jeremiah Mayfield. “And if you want people to trust you and trust law enforcement, then clearly label things, just like they do with the red-light cameras. They’re clearly labeled, they’re obvious, you know where they are.”

headlines.title: Zuckerberg distances Meta from calls for a coordinated approach on an AI slowdown
headlines.description: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said it’s up to each AI company to make sure its technology is safe, distancing himself from calls by rival companies for a coordinated slowdown in the development of advanced artificial intelligence. The comments Zuckerberg posted on social media followed a proposal from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that quickly found support from tech leaders including OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk at SpaceXAI. Warnings from researchers about the technology’s potential threats to humanity have sparked a debate among industry leaders over how best to rein in the technology before it could escape human control. AI companies are already motivated to develop their models in a safe way and face “significant liability” to prevent them from causing harm, Zuckerberg said. “Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely, and the ability to take its own actions to ensure that happens,” he wrote on X. Zuckerberg, who didn’t name Anthropic or any other companies, posted days after Amodei outlined a three-step plan to ensure AI safety, including a proposal for companies and countries to coordinate a slowdown in its development. Zuckerberg said Meta delayed releasing its Muse AI agent for several months to ensure its safety and security. “We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would,” he said. Companies should prioritize building safe AI models instead of systems that can automatically improve themselves, a function known as recursive self-improvement, Zuckerberg wrote. “Committing the significant majority of compute towards serving people rather than racing towards recursive self-improvement is one of the best ways to ensure we develop this technology safely.” Artificial intelligence Sep 12 Artificial intelligence Sep 9 Anthropic researcher resigns with a warning: AI ‘could kill us all'

headlines.title: Downtown San Jose bar owners hit with thousands in vandalism repairs
headlines.description: Downtown San Jose bar owners are grappling with frequent and senseless vandalism, forcing business operators to constantly shell out hundreds or thousands of dollars for repairs — ranging from exterior tagging to carved mirrors in restrooms. “It’s going to be over a thousand dollars to replace this mirror,” said George Lahlouh, who owns five bars and restaurants in downtown San Jose, including Alter Ego, Still OG and Miniboss. On Sunday, someone used a razor blade or knife to carve letters into a restroom mirror at Alter Ego. Lahlouh says vandals repeatedly target his businesses by tagging restrooms, destroying furniture with knives and painting graffiti on storefronts. He is not alone. At Cash Only, owner Cache Bouren says this bar and two others he owns downtown have also been targeted with people carving up sinks and restrooms. “Always tagging in the mirrors, carving into the walls and sinks,” Bouren said. “I’ve replaced the sinks three times in the last two years. They’re carving so deep in the sinks I can’t fix it.” The cleanup costs are adding up quickly for local business owners. Bouren estimates spending a minimum of $10,000 to $15,000 a year just to keep tags from becoming the main feature in the bathrooms. Bouren has chosen not to report the vandalism to police, noting, “We know the San Jose Police Department is understaffed and cannot invest resources in tracking these guys down.” To cope with the damage, Bouren has made adjustments by putting up protective shields and removing all mirrors from the restrooms. However, that measure did not stop vandals from etching into a hallway mirror instead. Lahlouh noted that the ongoing damage has sadly become a new cost of doing business. “Our colleagues are already challenged managing costs that are at an all-time high, and now we have to use funds on something avoidable,” Lahlouh said. “It’s super frustrating.”

headlines.title: Mountain View's Century 16 movie theatre to close
headlines.description: An iconic Mountain View movie theater is set to close its doors next week. The Century 16 theaters on North Shoreline Boulevard will officially close next Thursday, according to The Mercury News. The closure will make way for a large redevelopment known as the Shoreline Gateway Project. Plans call for a multi-building residential complex built around a central park. It remains unclear whether a movie theater will be included in the new development.

headlines.title: San Francisco mayor backs Prop H as Muni faces $307M budget shortfall
headlines.description: San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie is urging voters to support a parcel tax aimed at addressing a $307 million budget shortfall facing Muni. Proposition H, which will appear on the Nov. 3 ballot, would raise money for the transit agency through an annual parcel tax. Without additional funding, Muni says it could eliminate 19 bus lines and a streetcar route while reducing the frequency of service. A report from the San Francisco Controller’s Office found that reductions in bus and rail service could have broader economic effects across the city. According to the report, home prices could drop by as much as 0.9%, or about $14,000. The report also found that if Proposition H passes, nearly 1,509 jobs could be created over 15 years and the measure could generate about $400 million in economic growth. If approved, owners of single-family homes and condominiums would pay an annual parcel tax of at least $129. The tax would be at least $249 for multifamily properties and $799 for businesses. Lurie spoke in support of the measure Wednesday outside San Francisco City Hall. “If this does not pass, we could see wait times double,” Lurie said. “We could see a cut to service by up to 30%. We will see more traffic and gridlock on our streets, which will stunt our economic recovery.” San Francisco voters will decide Proposition H in the Nov. 3 general election. The city confirms that local ballot measures will be decided in that election.

headlines.title: Richmond becomes 3rd Bay Area city to impose data center moratorium
headlines.description: Richmond has become the third Bay Area city recently to temporarily halt new data center development, following Oakley and Gilroy, as its officials take time to study the potential impacts of the rapidly growing industry. The Richmond City Council voted Tuesday night to establish a 45-day moratorium on new data center development. The pause gives city officials time to study potential impacts and consider permanent protections before a project is proposed within city limits. Supporters of the moratorium said it allows Richmond officials to take a closer look at possible demands on the city’s electricity and water systems, as well as concerns about pollution and potential infrastructure and utility costs for residents. Shiva Mishek, a Richmond resident and program director with California-based environmental justice nonprofit Communities for a Better Environment, praised the council’s vote and said the city should work toward permanent protections. “As a community already on the frontlines of Chevron’s refinery pollution, we applaud the Richmond City Council for taking a proactive step to curb the rushed buildout of data centers,” Mishek said in a statement released by the city. Richmond residents and environmental advocates have raised concerns about the potential effects of data centers on pollution, electricity demand, water use and utility costs. Emi Yoko-Young, a policy organizer with clean energy advocacy coalition Reclaim Our Power: Utility Justice Campaign, said data centers are driving up energy bills around the country. “PG&E customers already pay some of the highest rates in the U.S. Today, Richmond took an important step toward protecting residents from further escalating power bills because of unchecked data center development,” Yoko-Young said. The 45-day moratorium will give Richmond time to evaluate potential data center development before any such project is proposed, city officials said. On Monday, Gilroy approved a 45-day moratorium on Monday on new data center applications. In March, the Oakley City Council approved an industrial development project that will turn vineyards into a logistics hub, but ditched the inclusion of data centers.

headlines.title: Well-preserved tooth from Pacific mastodon found in Bay Area creek
headlines.description: Brigid Lynch was working along a wooded creek in a mountainous part of the Bay Area when something that didn’t look like the rocks she’d been studying caught her eye. It turned out to be the fossilized tooth of a Pacific mastodon. “I keep joking it wasn’t hard to find,” Lynch, a geomorphologist at Balance Hydrologics, said Friday. “It was just sitting there in the middle of the creek, halfway in, half out of the water.” Lynch made the discovery earlier this year while working on a habitat restoration project for the threatened California red-legged frog in a Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District preserve in San Mateo County. The public land management agency that preserves over 70,000 acres of land in the Santa Cruz Mountains region announced the find this week. The fossil has been donated to Stanford University’s Doerr School of Sustainability. “It’s in great condition,” said Chrissy Garcia, curator and manager of Doerr School of Sustainability’s specimen collections. “So we’ve got both the crown and the root of the fossil. You can even see root canal.” “It’s exciting to have a specimen of this quality, and having it be a local find,” she said. Garcia said the tooth from the Pacific mastodon, an extinct elephantlike species, is about 9 inches (23 centimeters) long. Ron Tykoski, vice president of science and curator of vertebrate paleontology at the Perot Museum of Nature and Science in Dallas, said mastodon fossils “pop up with some degree of frequency, depending on where you live.” He said there are multiple species of mastodon that roamed for a few million years in North America, up till 10,000 to 12,000 years ago. “The way this was found is actually the way a lot of specimens are found, just somebody who happened to be in the right place,” Tykoski said. Garcia said that they’ll likely try to determine the exact age of the fossil, and will make a 3D copy to give to the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District. The district says it will use the copy for public outreach and education. Ryan McCauley, a spokesperson for the district, said the discovery on land they are preserving helps show the value of protecting open spaces and habitats. “That this tooth, that this molar, was found in the context of trying to protect the habitat and save another species from potentially going extinct I think really just drives home the point of why it’s so important to care for these open spaces and these natural lands,” he said.
